title: Advanced Powerlifting Workout: 8 Exercises for Maximum Strength
description: A 70-minute advanced strength session built around the powerlifting big three — squat, bench, deadlift — plus targeted accessory work for experienced lifters chasing new personal records. Periodized for peak force output, not pump.
text:
At the advanced level, strength training is no longer about learning movements or building a foundation. Those phases are behind you. The challenge shifts to something harder: extracting progress from a nervous system and musculature that have already adapted extensively to heavy loading, and doing so without accumulating the kind of systemic fatigue that derails a training block entirely.

This 70-minute session is structured around the powerlifting competition lifts — back squat, bench press, and conventional deadlift — because these movements produce the highest neuromuscular demand and the broadest systemic strength adaptations of any exercises available. They are supplemented by carefully selected accessory movements that address the specific weak points and structural demands of each primary lift.

The loading structure follows an intensity periodization model appropriate for advanced lifters: primary movements are trained at 85–95% of estimated one-rep max for low-rep clusters (2–3 reps), with the goal of maximizing neural drive and absolute force production rather than metabolic fatigue. At this percentage, the body is recruiting nearly all available motor units at near-maximum firing rates — this is the training stimulus that produces genuine strength gains in experienced athletes, as opposed to hypertrophy stimulus which requires higher volume and moderate intensity.

Rest periods on primary movements are 3–5 minutes. This is not negotiable at advanced loads. Full phosphocreatine replenishment requires at least 3 minutes between near-maximal efforts, and attempting the next set before full recovery produces a set that is neurologically compromised — you are not training maximum strength, you are training the fatigue of maximum strength, which is a different and less productive stimulus. Accessory movements use 90-second to 2-minute rest periods.

RPE (Rate of Perceived Exertion) is your primary loading tool throughout this session. Target RPE 8–9 on primary movements — meaning you should feel you have 1–2 reps in reserve at the end of each set. If a set feels like RPE 10 or you grind significantly, take extra rest before the next attempt and consider reducing load by 2.5–5%. Grinding heavy singles teaches poor motor patterns under fatigue. Speed and technique must be preserved even at near-maximal loads.

The accessory block addresses the most common strength limiters for advanced lifters: posterior chain weakness limiting squat depth and deadlift lockout, tricep strength limiting bench press lockout, and upper back weakness creating breakdown in the squat rack position. Every accessory exercise in this program has a direct mechanical relationship to one of the primary lifts — none is selected for aesthetic reasons.

Deload every fourth week: reduce all working weights to 60% of normal session loads and perform the same movements with the same structure. Accumulated fatigue masks fitness in advanced athletes more significantly than in beginners — you will often set personal records in the week following a deload, not the week of the heaviest training. This is counterintuitive and consistently true.

Progression at the advanced level is measured in months, not sessions. A 2.5 kg increase to your competition squat over 12 weeks of focused training is excellent progress. Attempting to add weight every session as an advanced lifter leads directly to stagnation and overreaching. Track every working set, every RPE rating, and your sleep quality — the correlation between sleep and next-day strength output is among the most robust findings in sports science, and at advanced loads, a poor night's sleep is a genuine reason to reduce session intensity rather than push through.
equipment: Barbell, Power Rack, Bench, Dumbbells, Cable Machine, Belt, Chalk
targetMuscleGroups: Quadriceps, Hamstrings, Glutes, Erector Spinae, Pectoralis Major, Triceps, Latissimus Dorsi, Trapezius

nutritionAdvice.preWorkout: Eat a substantial meal 90–120 minutes before training — this is not a session to approach underfueled. Target 60–80g of complex carbohydrates and 35–45g of lean protein: white rice with chicken breast and sweet potato, whole grain pasta with tuna, or oatmeal with two whole eggs and a scoop of whey. Carbohydrate availability is directly linked to maximal force output through the phosphocreatine and glycolytic systems — sub-optimal glycogen status measurably reduces strength on working sets above 85% of one-rep max. If you use creatine monohydrate (5g daily), take it consistently — at this training intensity, creatine supplementation produces its most significant performance effects. Avoid high-fiber foods and large fat servings in the 90 minutes before training to minimize gastrointestinal discomfort under heavy abdominal bracing.
nutritionAdvice.postWorkout: Within 30–45 minutes of finishing, consume 40–50g of fast-digesting protein combined with 70–90g of simple or moderate-glycemic carbohydrates. At advanced training volumes and intensities, muscle protein synthesis rates are significantly elevated post-session and the anabolic window is meaningful — do not skip this meal. Whey protein with white rice and banana, a large serving of Greek yogurt with granola and honey, or a full meal of lean protein with white potato or rice all work effectively. For a session this demanding, total daily caloric intake matters as much as the post-workout meal: advanced strength athletes typically require 3,000–4,500 kcal daily depending on body weight and training volume to support recovery and strength adaptation. Chronic undereating is the most common reason advanced lifters plateau.
nutritionAdvice.hydration: Drink 600–750ml of water in the 2 hours before training. During a 70-minute high-intensity strength session, consume 250–350ml every 15–20 minutes — total intra-workout intake should be 800ml to 1L. Dehydration of 2% of body weight produces a measurable reduction in maximal force output and coordination — at near-maximal loads, this directly affects both performance and safety. Add an electrolyte supplement or dissolve 500mg of sodium in your intra-workout water for sessions involving significant sweating or warm training environments: sodium drives fluid retention in active tissues and maintains neuromuscular signaling efficiency. After training, drink a minimum of 750ml within 45 minutes and continue drinking throughout the remainder of the day — a 70-minute session at this intensity can produce 1–2L of fluid loss through sweat depending on body size and conditions.

exercises.name: Barbell Back Squat
exercises.technique: Set the barbell on a power rack at mid-chest height. Step under it and position it across your upper traps — high bar for quad emphasis, low bar (rear deltoids) for greater hip and posterior chain involvement. Grip the bar just outside shoulder width and create maximal full-body tension before unracking: chest up, lats engaged hard, core braced with a Valsalva maneuver. Unrack with control and walk out with the minimum steps necessary — two steps back, feet set at shoulder width with toes angled 15–30 degrees outward. Take a deep diaphragmatic breath into your belly, brace as if absorbing a punch, and hold that brace for the entire rep. Initiate the descent by pushing knees out and sitting the hips back simultaneously. Descend with control to below parallel — hip crease clearly below the top of the knee. Drive out of the hole with maximum intent, maintaining the brace and bar path. Lock out fully at the top before exhaling and setting up for the next rep.
exercises.tips: At 85–95% intensity, treat every rep as a technical single — reset your brace completely between reps in the rack if needed. Bar speed on the concentric phase is the primary indicator of neural readiness: if the bar moves slowly on the first rep at your working weight, take additional rest before the next set. Use a belt at these percentages — it does not replace core activation, it enhances it by giving the core something to brace against, allowing 10–15% higher intra-abdominal pressure than unbelted lifting.
exercises.commonMistakes: Good morning squat — hips rising faster than the chest out of the hole, which shifts the load entirely to the posterior chain and places extreme stress on the lumbar spine. Knees caving under maximal load — this indicates the abductors and glutes are insufficiently strong relative to the working weight. Losing upper back tightness on heavy sets, causing the bar to roll forward and the torso to collapse.
exercises.muscles: Quadriceps, Gluteus Maximus, Hamstrings, Adductors, Erector Spinae, Core, Upper Back

exercises.name: Pause Squat
exercises.technique: Set up and descend exactly as in the competition back squat. At the bottom position — at or just below parallel — stop completely and hold the position for a full 2–3 second count. There must be zero bounce, zero elastic rebound: the pause eliminates the stretch-shortening cycle and forces the muscles to generate force from a dead stop. The pause should be genuinely static — if you feel yourself sinking further during the pause, brace harder. After the full count, drive out of the bottom with maximum acceleration. Use 70–75% of your working back squat weight for these sets — the pause dramatically increases the difficulty relative to the load on the bar.
exercises.tips: The pause squat is the single most effective squat accessory for advanced lifters because it directly targets the sticking point — the transition from the eccentric to concentric phase — which is where the majority of missed squats fail. It also forces honest depth: you cannot bounce out of a partial squat when you are required to hold the bottom position. The 2–3 second pause is a minimum; longer pauses increase the stimulus further.
exercises.commonMistakes: Using a bounce at the bottom instead of a true static pause — this defeats the entire purpose of the variation. Using too much weight and losing position during the pause — technique must be completely solid during the hold. Exhaling during the pause, which deflates core pressure exactly when maximum bracing is required.
exercises.muscles: Quadriceps, Gluteus Maximus, Hamstrings, Adductors, Core, Erector Spinae

exercises.name: Barbell Bench Press
exercises.technique: Lie on a flat bench with eyes directly under the bar. Grip the bar at a width where your forearms are vertical when the bar touches your chest — typically just outside shoulder width for most lifters. Retract and depress your shoulder blades maximally and press them hard into the bench — maintain this position for the entire set without exception. Create a moderate arch in the lower back with both feet flat on the floor, generating leg drive by pressing the floor away and driving your traps into the bench. Unrack the bar and position it directly over the lower chest. Lower with full control to your lower sternum, keeping elbows at 45–55 degrees from the torso. Touch the chest with control — no bounce — then drive the bar upward with maximum force intent, finishing with arms locked out over your lower chest. Rack only after complete lockout.
exercises.tips: At near-maximal loads, setup is 50% of the lift. Spending 15–20 seconds establishing correct shoulder blade retraction, leg drive, and bar position before unracking produces meaningfully better performance than rushing. Squeeze the bar as if trying to bend it throughout the set — this activates the forearm and tricep musculature maximally and creates full-arm rigidity. Leg drive is not optional at advanced loads: pressing your feet into the floor and driving force through your traps creates a stable rigid base that allows 5–10% more force transfer to the bar.
exercises.commonMistakes: Losing shoulder blade retraction as fatigue accumulates — the shoulder rolling forward is both a performance limiter and a primary injury mechanism for the anterior shoulder under heavy load. Bouncing the bar off the chest to complete a rep — at these intensities this creates significant impact stress and compensates for the actual pressing weakness rather than addressing it. Bar path drifting over the face at lockout rather than finishing over the lower chest, which indicates tricep weakness is the limiting factor.
exercises.muscles: Pectoralis Major, Anterior Deltoid, Triceps Brachii, Serratus Anterior

exercises.name: Close-Grip Bench Press
exercises.technique: Set up identically to the competition bench press but move your grip inward so your index fingers are on the smooth ring of the bar, or slightly inside your competition grip width. This narrower grip shifts the emphasis to the triceps and front deltoids, directly training the lockout strength that limits most advanced benchers at the top of the movement. Retract shoulder blades, create leg drive, and arch as in competition setup. Lower the bar to the mid-chest or slightly higher than your competition touch point, keeping elbows close to the torso — more tucked than your competition press. Drive to full lockout with maximum acceleration. Use 75–80% of your competition bench weight for working sets.
exercises.tips: The close-grip bench is the highest-specificity tricep exercise available to a powerlifter because it trains the triceps in the exact position and through the exact range of motion they are required to work in during the competition lift. Skull crushers and pushdowns develop the muscle; the close-grip bench develops the movement. Do not go narrower than index-finger-on-smooth-ring — an excessively narrow grip creates wrist and elbow stress without additional tricep benefit.
exercises.commonMistakes: Gripping too narrow — hands touching or shoulder-width or less — which strains the wrists and elbows and limits the load you can use effectively. Flaring the elbows outward during the set, which simply reverts the movement back toward a standard bench press. Reducing the range of motion to avoid fatigue rather than pressing to full lockout on every rep.
exercises.muscles: Triceps Brachii, Anterior Deltoid, Pectoralis Major (medial), Anconeus

exercises.name: Conventional Deadlift
exercises.technique: Approach the bar with feet hip-width apart, bar directly over mid-foot — 2–3 cm from your shins. Hinge at the hips and grip just outside your legs with either a double overhand, hook grip, or mixed grip. Set your hip angle — hips higher than a squat but lower than a hip hinge — so your shoulders are slightly in front of the bar. Take all slack out of the bar by pulling upward until the plates move but before they leave the floor: you will hear a click. This pre-tension is essential at maximal loads to prevent a sudden jerk that loads the lumbar spine unprepared. Take a full Valsalva breath, brace maximally, then drive your feet through the floor while simultaneously pulling the bar into your body. The bar must stay in contact with your legs throughout — if it drifts forward, the lever arm increases exponentially. Lock out by driving hips forward and squeezing glutes — not by hyperextending the lumbar spine. Lower under control: do not drop from height.
exercises.tips: At advanced loads, the Valsalva maneuver is non-negotiable — intra-abdominal pressure at near-maximal deadlift loads is the primary spinal protection mechanism, and a loose brace under 200kg+ is a genuine injury risk. Use chalk on every working set — grip failure under heavy loads is dangerous and avoidable. If using a mixed grip, alternate which hand supinates between warm-up sets to prevent bicep tendon adaptation asymmetry.
exercises.commonMistakes: Jerking the bar off the floor rather than building tension first — this applies a sudden impulse load to the lumbar spine rather than a controlled force. Allowing the bar to drift forward from the body mid-lift, which creates a progressively longer lever arm and shifts the majority of load to the lower back. Hyperextending the spine at lockout rather than achieving a neutral standing position — this is not strength, it is spinal compression.
exercises.muscles: Hamstrings, Gluteus Maximus, Erector Spinae, Trapezius, Latissimus Dorsi, Quadriceps, Forearms, Core

exercises.name: Romanian Deadlift
exercises.technique: Take the barbell from a rack at hip height with a double overhand grip, shoulder width. Stand with feet hip-width apart. Push your hips directly backward while maintaining a soft knee bend — the movement is a hip hinge, not a squat. Lower the bar along your thighs, keeping it in contact with your legs throughout the descent. Your back remains completely flat: chest up, shoulders back, neutral spine from cervical to lumbar. Descend until you feel maximal hamstring tension — for most advanced lifters this is at or below mid-shin — then reverse by driving the hips forward. Squeeze the glutes hard at the top. The Romanian deadlift should be performed with a 3-second controlled eccentric at advanced level — the slow descent maximizes hamstring mechanical tension and produces the posterior chain hypertrophy that supports heavier competition deadlifts.
exercises.tips: Load the Romanian deadlift heavier than most programs suggest — advanced lifters can use 60–70% of their conventional deadlift max here because the range of motion is shorter and there is no floor contact to manage. The hamstrings are the primary speed limiter in the conventional deadlift below the knee: making them stronger and more resilient through heavy RDL work directly translates to heavier pulling numbers within 6–8 weeks.
exercises.commonMistakes: Rounding the lower back to achieve greater range of motion — the depth is entirely determined by hamstring flexibility under a neutral spine. Bending the knees excessively, which converts the hip hinge into a partial deadlift and removes tension from the hamstrings. Losing bar contact with the legs during the descent, which dramatically increases spinal loading.
exercises.muscles: Hamstrings, Gluteus Maximus, Erector Spinae, Adductor Magnus, Forearms

exercises.name: Barbell Bent-Over Row
exercises.technique: Stand over the barbell with feet hip-width apart. Hinge to a torso angle of 45–60 degrees from the floor and grip the bar overhand at just outside shoulder width. Brace your entire trunk — this position creates significant spinal loading and requires the same core engagement as the deadlift. Pull the bar toward your lower sternum by driving your elbows back and up, retracting your shoulder blades maximally at the top. Hold the contracted position for a half-second before lowering with full control over 2–3 seconds. Your torso angle must remain constant throughout — do not use a torso swing to generate momentum. Use a belt on your heaviest sets.
exercises.tips: The barbell row at this loading level is as much a lower back and core exercise as it is a back exercise. Treat the hip hinge position as a plank — maintain it with the same intent you would maintain form on a deadlift. At advanced loads, the bent-over row directly reinforces the lat and upper back strength required to maintain the squat rack position and prevent bar drift in the deadlift.
exercises.commonMistakes: Using torso momentum to swing the bar rather than maintaining a fixed hinge angle — this reduces upper back stimulus and creates cumulative spinal fatigue. Pulling to the wrong point on the torso: too high (toward the neck) overloads the rear deltoid; too low (toward the navel) reduces lat engagement. Rushing the eccentric and losing the controlled lowering that provides the majority of the hypertrophic stimulus.
exercises.muscles: Latissimus Dorsi, Rhomboids, Middle Trapezius, Rear Deltoid, Biceps Brachii, Erector Spinae, Core

exercises.name: Weighted Plank
exercises.technique: Set up in a standard forearm plank — elbows directly under shoulders, forearms flat and parallel, toes curled under, body forming a straight line from head to heels. Have a training partner place a weight plate (10–20kg) on your upper back, centered between the shoulder blades. Brace your core with maximum intent — squeeze quads, glutes, and pull your navel toward your spine simultaneously. Hold for the full 45 seconds with no sagging of the hips or elevation of the glutes. Breathe in a shallow, controlled pattern — do not deflate your core brace with a full exhalation. Remove the plate before standing.
exercises.tips: At advanced loads, core anti-extension strength — the ability to resist lumbar extension under load — is the limiting factor in both squat and deadlift performance, not the prime movers themselves. The weighted plank trains this quality isometrically with a load that significantly exceeds what bodyweight planks provide for an experienced athlete. Start with 10kg and increase by 5kg as 45 seconds becomes manageable without form breakdown.
exercises.commonMistakes: Allowing the hips to pike upward to offload the core — the body must remain completely rigid. Placing the weight too high toward the neck or too low toward the lower back, which creates imbalanced spinal loading. Holding the breath for the entire set instead of maintaining shallow controlled breathing, which creates unnecessary cardiovascular stress.
exercises.muscles: Transverse Abdominis, Rectus Abdominis, Obliques, Erector Spinae, Gluteus Maximus, Quadriceps
